newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Israel insists it committed to peace.
newsitem.headline: Israel insists it committed to peace.

text.p: Israel, buoyed by its firm stance at the Middle East crisis summit in Washington, insisted on Thursday it remained committed to peace but said it would not allow its security to be threatened.

Foreign Minister David Levy, in a speech to the U.N. General Assembly one day after the Washington summit, offered no new initiatives on negotiations with the Palestinians or Arab countries in the region.

But he said suspicions in the Arab world and in Europe that Israel's new right-wing government was determined to block moves towards Middle East peace were unfounded, despite the worst crisis since the process began five years ago.
"Once again, from this great podium, I wish to reaffirm Israel's irreversible commitment and determination to pursue the path of peace," Levy said.

"Shall we opt for cooperation, progress, real peace and security, or will we revert to the sombre days of conflict, confrontation and violence, putting an end to all hope? Israel, for its part, has chosen hope."
Israel hailed the Washington summit as a victory for its firm stance, but Palestinians called it a failure.
Following clashes in the West Bank and Gaza in which 58 Palestinians and 15 Israelis have died, the summit's only real agreement was to continue negotiations between the two sides.
Levy thanked the United States, Israel's chief ally, for its role in brokering the talks between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
"We recognise that we bear a heavy responsibility to our people and to the whole region," Levy said.
"We recognise that we must all display good faith and mutual understanding in order to fulfil our mission and to send out the message that stable peace and durable security can be achieved."
Levy called on Syria to resume peace negotiations with Israel and he paid tribute to other Arab countries, including Egypt, Jordan and Morocco for their role.

Arab countries have accused Israel's new government of giving up the principle of "land for peace" espoused by the previous Labour government, and of failing to implement previous agreements reached with the Palestinians.

Levy said Israel was committed to reducing military tensions in the region, determined to keep negotiations with the Palestinians free from violence and to ensure the security of the Jewish state as a guiding principle.
"Security is neither an obsession nor a blind belief. It touches upon our very existence in a region where threats and instability still rage," he said.
"Security must be the cornerstone of the edifice of peace. It cannot, under any circumstances, be held hostage to a process where terrorism, violence or armed conflict have not said their last word."
